note: 50 questions, all one level. Built for surprise while staying guessable. Every citation points at a source retrieved during research.

questions.prompt: How many people still lack safely managed drinking water?
questions.whyCorrect: 2.2 billion people — more than one in four of us — can't rely on safe water at home.
questions.action: Count how many times you used clean water today.

questions.prompt: How many people lack safely managed sanitation — a safe toilet?
questions.whyCorrect: 3.4 billion people — over 40% of the world. Sanitation lags even further behind water.
questions.action: Ask what happens to waste where there's no sewer or safe toilet.

questions.prompt: How many people can't wash their hands with soap and water at home?
questions.whyCorrect: 1.7 billion people. Handwashing is the cheapest disease prevention there is, and a fifth of the world can't do it at home.
questions.action: Count the handwashing spots in your home.

questions.prompt: What share of the world has safely managed drinking water?
questions.whyCorrect: 74%, up from 68% in 2015. Real progress — and still 2.2 billion people short.
whyWrong: Too optimistic — over a quarter lack safe water.
Too pessimistic — nearly three-quarters have it.
questions.action: Compare 68% in 2015 with 74% today.

questions.prompt: What share of the world has safely managed sanitation?
questions.whyCorrect: 58%, up from 48% in 2015. Sanitation improved faster than water in percentage terms, but from a much lower base.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — most people have it.
questions.action: Ask why sanitation lags behind drinking water.

questions.prompt: Since 1970, freshwater species populations have declined by:
questions.whyCorrect: 83% — the steepest decline of any group of species on Earth. Rivers and lakes have been hit harder than oceans or forests.
questions.action: Look up one freshwater species that's disappearing near you.

questions.prompt: What share of freshwater fish species are at risk of extinction?
questions.whyCorrect: A quarter of all freshwater fish species are threatened with extinction.
whyWrong: Too high, though the real figure is alarming.
questions.action: Name a fish that lives in fresh water near you.

questions.prompt: How much of the world's domestic wastewater is safely treated before being released?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 56% of the 332 billion cubic metres we produce. Nearly half of household wastewater goes back into the environment untreated.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — just over half is treated.
questions.action: Find out where your household's wastewater goes.

questions.prompt: How many children go to a school with no basic drinking water?
questions.whyCorrect: 447 million children have no basic drinking water at school — 77% of schools have it, meaning nearly a quarter don't.
questions.action: Ask how you'd concentrate all day without water.

questions.prompt: How many children are at schools with no basic hygiene facilities?
questions.whyCorrect: 646 million children — only 67% of schools provide basic hygiene like handwashing.
questions.action: Check whether there's soap in your school's bathrooms.

questions.prompt: Global water stress has changed how much since 2015?
questions.whyCorrect: Water stress has been flat at 18% since 2015 — no progress at all on one of Goal 6's central measures.
whyWrong: It has been stable, not soaring.
questions.action: Ask what 'water stress' actually measures.

questions.prompt: What share of people live with high or critical water stress?
questions.whyCorrect: 10% of the world's population — around 800 million people living where water demand seriously outstrips supply.
whyWrong: Too low by a factor of ten.
Too high — though water stress affects many regions.
questions.action: Look up whether your region is water-stressed.

questions.prompt: Which region's water stress got significantly worse since 2015?
questions.whyCorrect: Northern Africa and Western Asia saw a 12% increase in water stress — already among the driest regions on Earth.
whyWrong: Not identified as a major worsening region in this data.
questions.action: Find that region on a map and note its climate.

questions.prompt: How efficiently the world uses water improved since 2015 by:
questions.whyCorrect: Water-use efficiency rose 23%, from $17.5 to $21.5 of economic value per cubic metre — we're getting more from every drop.
questions.action: Think of one way to get more use from the same water.

questions.prompt: What share of schools have basic sanitation?
questions.whyCorrect: 78% — leaving 427 million children at schools with no proper toilet.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — most schools have sanitation.
Too optimistic — over a fifth of schools lack it.
questions.action: Ask why school toilets matter especially for girls.

questions.prompt: Basic hygiene at home reaches what share of people?
questions.whyCorrect: 80%, up sharply from 66% in 2015 — one of the fastest improvements in Goal 6, partly driven by COVID-era handwashing campaigns.
whyWrong: Too optimistic — 1.7 billion people still lack it.
Too pessimistic — four in five have it.
questions.action: Ask what changed about handwashing after 2020.

questions.prompt: How much domestic wastewater does the world produce each year?
questions.whyCorrect: 332 billion cubic metres — and only 56% of it is safely treated before returning to rivers, lakes and seas.
questions.action: Ask what untreated wastewater does to a river.

questions.prompt: Between water and sanitation, which is further behind?
questions.whyCorrect: Sanitation at 58% trails water at 74%. Toilets and sewers cost more and are politically less popular than taps.
questions.action: Ask why a government might build taps before toilets.

questions.prompt: Freshwater species have fallen 83% since 1970. How does that compare to other habitats?
options: It's the steepest decline of any habitat
questions.whyCorrect: Freshwater has been hit harder than land or ocean habitats — rivers and lakes are small, easily polluted, and heavily dammed.
whyWrong: It's the most severe decline recorded.
questions.action: Ask what a dam does to fish that migrate.

questions.prompt: Safe drinking water coverage rose from 68% to 74% in nine years. At that pace, will everyone have it by 2030?
questions.whyCorrect: About 0.7 points a year with 26 points to go means roughly 37 more years. Goal 6 will be missed by decades at this pace.
whyWrong: The required pace is several times faster.
The gap is far too large.
questions.action: Do the arithmetic: 26 points at 0.7 a year.

questions.prompt: Roughly what share of the world lacks a safe toilet?
questions.whyCorrect: With 58% covered, over 40% — some 3.4 billion people — lack safely managed sanitation.
whyWrong: Too high — most people do have safe sanitation.
questions.action: Ask what 'safely managed' adds to just 'having a toilet'.

questions.prompt: Why does handwashing matter so much for health?
options: It's the cheapest way to stop disease spreading
questions.whyCorrect: Handwashing with soap prevents diarrhoeal and respiratory infections cheaply and effectively — and 1.7 billion people can't do it at home.
whyWrong: Household handwashing prevents a large share of childhood illness.
It's among the most effective public health measures known.
questions.action: Time yourself washing hands properly — 20 seconds.

questions.prompt: Water-use efficiency is measured as:
options: Economic value produced per cubic metre
questions.whyCorrect: It's the economic value generated per cubic metre of water — currently $21.5, up from $17.5 in 2015.
whyWrong: Infrastructure count isn't the efficiency measure.
questions.action: Ask which uses more water: a T-shirt or a burger?

questions.prompt: How many children have no basic sanitation at school?
questions.whyCorrect: 427 million children — and 447 million lack drinking water at school.
questions.action: Ask what a student does all day with no school toilet.

questions.prompt: Global water stress sits at 18%. Is that improving?
questions.whyCorrect: Completely flat since 2015. Rising demand has cancelled out every efficiency gain.
questions.action: Ask how efficiency can rise while stress stays flat.

questions.prompt: Which improved fastest since 2015?
questions.whyCorrect: Hygiene jumped 14 percentage points — faster than sanitation's 10 or water's 6, helped by the pandemic's focus on handwashing.
whyWrong: Sanitation rose 10 points, still less than hygiene.
Water rose 6 points, the slowest of the three.
questions.action: Ask whether a crisis can accelerate good change.

questions.prompt: A quarter of freshwater fish species face extinction. What's driving it?
questions.whyCorrect: Freshwater habitats are polluted by untreated wastewater — 44% of it globally — dammed, drained and overfished, all at once.
whyWrong: Nearly half of wastewater is released untreated.
questions.action: Look up what lives in your nearest river.

questions.prompt: Which is true about school water and sanitation?
options: Roughly a quarter of schools lack water or toilets
questions.whyCorrect: 77% have drinking water and 78% have sanitation — so roughly a quarter of the world's schools lack one or both.
whyWrong: Hundreds of millions of children attend schools without them.
questions.action: Ask how many schools in your area would fail that test.

questions.prompt: Sanitation coverage rose 10 points since 2015. How many still lack it?
questions.whyCorrect: 3.4 billion people. Even after a decade of the fastest sanitation progress on record, over 40% of humanity is uncovered.
questions.action: Compare 3.4 billion with the world population.

questions.prompt: What does 'safely managed' drinking water mean?
options: Available at home, when needed, and free from contamination
questions.whyCorrect: It must be accessible at home, available when needed, and free from contamination — a much higher bar than simply having a water source somewhere.
whyWrong: Untreated or distant sources don't count.
Piped and protected sources both count; bottled isn't required.
questions.action: Check your water against all three tests.

questions.prompt: Freshwater species declined 83% since 1970. Roughly how many decades is that?
questions.whyCorrect: Around five decades — a collapse within a single human lifetime.
questions.action: Ask someone born before 1970 what local rivers were like.

questions.prompt: How much water-related economic value does each cubic metre now generate?
questions.whyCorrect: $21.5 per cubic metre, up from $17.5 in 2015 — a 23% efficiency improvement.
questions.action: Ask which industries use the most water per dollar earned.

questions.prompt: Which group of people is most affected by a lack of school toilets?
questions.whyCorrect: With 427 million children at schools without sanitation, girls are disproportionately affected — many miss school entirely during menstruation.
whyWrong: The impact falls unevenly, especially on girls.
It affects all students, but girls face the sharpest barrier.
questions.action: Ask what a school needs so nobody misses days.

questions.prompt: Nearly half of wastewater goes untreated. Where does it end up?
questions.whyCorrect: Untreated wastewater flows into freshwater systems and oceans — a major driver of the 83% collapse in freshwater species.
whyWrong: There's no such containment at scale.
It carries pollutants that don't simply vanish.
questions.action: Trace where your nearest river flows to.

questions.prompt: Water stress affects 10% of people at high or critical levels. What does that mean day to day?
questions.whyCorrect: It means a region is withdrawing far more water than is being replenished — leading to rationing, falling groundwater and dry rivers.
whyWrong: Water stress is about scarcity, not excess.
questions.action: Ask what your area does during a drought.

questions.prompt: Basic hygiene coverage went from 66% to 80%. How many still lack it?
questions.whyCorrect: 1.7 billion people still can't wash their hands with soap and water at home, despite the fastest improvement of any Goal 6 measure.
questions.action: Ask what soap costs where you live.

questions.prompt: Which Goal 6 measure has made NO progress since 2015?
questions.whyCorrect: Water stress has been stuck at 18% for a decade, while water, sanitation and hygiene coverage all improved.
questions.action: Ask why scarcity is harder to fix than access.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many people is 10% of the world facing critical water stress?
questions.whyCorrect: Roughly 800 million people — comparable to the number living in extreme poverty.
questions.action: Convert percentages into people whenever you read them.

questions.prompt: What share of schools provide basic hygiene facilities?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 67% — the weakest of the three school measures, behind water (77%) and sanitation (78%).
whyWrong: Too optimistic — a third of schools lack them.
Too pessimistic — two-thirds do have them.
questions.action: Compare 67%, 77% and 78% for schools.

questions.prompt: How much did safe drinking water coverage improve between 2015 and 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: From 68% to 74% — six points in nine years, far too slow for universal coverage by 2030.
questions.action: Ask what would speed this up.

questions.prompt: Which is bigger: people without safe water, or people without safe sanitation?
questions.whyCorrect: 1.2 billion more people lack safe sanitation than lack safe water. Toilets are the bigger unfinished job.
questions.action: Ask why sanitation is harder to deliver than water.

questions.prompt: Freshwater covers a tiny share of Earth's surface but holds:
options: A quarter of species now at risk of extinction
questions.whyCorrect: 25% of freshwater fish species are threatened, and freshwater populations overall have fallen 83% since 1970 — disproportionate loss in a small habitat.
whyWrong: A quarter of freshwater fish species are threatened.
Freshwater holds insects, amphibians, plants and mammals too.
questions.action: Name three non-fish animals that live in fresh water.

questions.prompt: Sanitation rose from 48% to 58%. What does that leave for 2030?
options: 42 points in six years — far off track
questions.whyCorrect: Ten points in nine years, with 42 to go. Universal sanitation by 2030 would need roughly seven times the current pace.
whyWrong: The target is a long way from being met.
questions.action: Work out the yearly rate needed to close 42 points by 2030.

questions.prompt: Northern Africa and Western Asia's water stress rose 12% since 2015. What does that suggest?
questions.whyCorrect: The regions with the least water are seeing demand grow fastest — climate change and population growth compounding existing scarcity.
whyWrong: The worsening is concentrated in already-arid regions.
Global stress is flat and this region's is rising.
questions.action: Look up the driest inhabited region on Earth.

questions.prompt: Which best describes Goal 6's overall progress?
questions.whyCorrect: Water, sanitation and hygiene access all rose — while freshwater species fell 83% and water stress didn't budge. Human access and nature are moving in opposite directions.
whyWrong: All three access measures are far off the 2030 targets.
Access to water, sanitation and hygiene all improved.
questions.action: Ask whether you can supply people and protect rivers at once.

questions.prompt: How many cubic metres of wastewater are safely treated each year?
questions.whyCorrect: 56% of 332 billion is roughly 186 billion cubic metres treated — leaving about 146 billion released untreated.
whyWrong: That's the total produced, not the amount treated.
questions.action: Work out 56% of 332 billion yourself.

questions.prompt: Only 67% of schools have hygiene facilities. What's the direct consequence?
options: 646 million children can't wash their hands at school
questions.whyCorrect: 646 million children attend schools with no basic hygiene — a major driver of illness and missed school days.
whyWrong: Handwashing access directly affects illness rates.
Schools operate without these facilities, which is the problem.
questions.action: Ask how often illness keeps students home at your school.

questions.prompt: Water-use efficiency improved 23% but stress stayed flat. Why?
options: Demand grew as fast as efficiency improved
questions.whyCorrect: Population and economic growth increased total demand, cancelling out the efficiency gains — a pattern seen across many environmental measures.
whyWrong: Water stress is tracked annually at 18%.
Efficiency reduces stress, all else equal.
questions.action: Ask where else efficiency gains get eaten by growth.

questions.prompt: Which of these numbers is largest?
questions.whyCorrect: Sanitation is the biggest gap at 3.4 billion, then water at 2.2 billion, then hygiene at 1.7 billion.
whyWrong: The smallest of the three, though still enormous.
Large, but 1.2 billion smaller than sanitation.
questions.action: Rank the three gaps and say which you'd fix first.

questions.prompt: What's the most surprising thing about Goal 6?
options: Freshwater life fell 83% while human access improved
questions.whyCorrect: Human access to water, sanitation and hygiene all rose since 2015 — while freshwater species collapsed by 83% and water stress stayed flat. Helping people and protecting nature aren't the same job.
whyWrong: All Goal 6 targets are badly off track for 2030.
Water, sanitation and hygiene coverage all improved measurably.
questions.action: Ask how a country could do both at once.
